Tanegashima Space Center, 2010-05-20. Shared a launch with the IKAROS solar-sail demonstrator (the first interplanetary solar sail) and four university small satellites. Akatsuki — "dawn" in Japanese — was Japan's first Venus mission, designed for a 30-month primary mission to study Venus atmospheric super-rotation.
H-IIA second stage delivers Akatsuki onto a direct 6-month transfer to Venus. The Orbit Maneuvering Engine (OME) was reserved for the planned VOI.
First mid-course correction during the nominal 2010 cruise.
2010-12-07. Akatsuki arrives at Venus and begins the planned VOI burn.
VOI-1 failure — salt-blocked helium check valve

Approximately 152 seconds into the planned 720-second VOI burn, the probe entered safe mode: salt deposits had blocked a check valve between the helium pressurant tank and the fuel tank, and the Orbit Maneuvering Engine, starved of fuel, ran oxidiser-rich and overheated. Akatsuki sailed past Venus into solar orbit. Recovery plan: keep the spacecraft alive in solar orbit until the next Venus encounter window (2015 or 2016), then attempt VOI again using the attitude-control thrusters.

Twelve correction maneuvers during the 5-year solar-orbit hold to re-phase the heliocentric trajectory for a 2015 Venus re-encounter. The main OME was tested in 2011 and found permanently damaged; planning shifted entirely to RCS-thruster-based VOI.
2015-12-07 — exactly five years after the first attempt. Akatsuki arrives at Venus again.

1228-second burn using four attitude-control thrusters (originally rated for ~50 m/s ∆v; ran 244 m/s) placed Akatsuki into a highly elliptical 400 × 440,000 km, 3°-inclination prograde orbit. JAXA confirmed VOI-R2 success the following day. The recovery is one of the most dramatic mission-saves in spaceflight history. Akatsuki mapped Venus's UV/IR cloud features, confirmed bow-shaped gravity waves above Aphrodite Terra, and provided continuous super-rotation tracking until contact was lost in 2024. JAXA declared operations complete on 2025-09-18.
Recovered from a 5-year solar-orbit hold to achieve Venus orbit on a backup attempt; the only Venus orbiter active in its final years of operation

Akatsuki — "dawn" — was Japan's first Venus mission. Launched 2010-05-20 from Tanegashima on an H-IIA 202, paired with the IKAROS solar-sail demonstrator. The planned Venus orbit insertion 2010-12-07 failed when salt deposits blocked a check valve between the helium pressurant tank and the fuel tank; the engine, starved of fuel, ran oxidiser-rich and overheated, and the probe entered safe mode about 152 seconds into the burn. JAXA kept the spacecraft alive in solar orbit for five years, twelve correction maneuvers, until the next Venus encounter window. On 2015-12-07 a 1228-second burn using four attitude-control thrusters — never designed for orbital insertion — placed Akatsuki into a highly elliptical 400 × 440,000 km, 3°-inclination orbit. One of the most dramatic mission-saves in spaceflight history. Contact was lost in 2024; JAXA declared operations complete on 2025-09-18.
